summary: Defines an SMTP extension that lets a client ask the server to deliver a message within a set period of time. It is on the standards track.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 2852 lets a mail sender state that a message should arrive within a given number of seconds, and say what the server should do if that time passes. The server either stops trying and reports failure, or keeps trying and reports a delay. The RFC is careful to say that this expresses urgency, not a request for faster handling.

subtitle: Lets a mail sender say by when a message must arrive, and what should happen if it does not.

tldr.problem: A sender often knows that a message matters only up to a certain time, but the mail servers handling it do not. Without a way to express that, a message can be delivered hours or days after it has stopped being useful, or the sender never learns that delivery failed.
tldr.mechanism: The client adds a BY parameter to the MAIL FROM command, giving a number of seconds and a mode. In return mode the server stops trying and reports a failed delivery notification when the time runs out; in notify mode it keeps trying and reports a delayed notification. The server can also advertise the smallest deadline it will accept.
tldr.outcome: The result is a documented way to express urgency and to withdraw a message that missed its deadline, together with a new Deliver-By-Date field in the delivery status notification. The RFC says plainly that this is not a request for priority processing.

today: RFC 2852 is a Proposed Standard from June 2000. It updates RFC 1894, the format of delivery status notifications, by adding a Deliver-By-Date field to the per-message fields, and it is not obsoleted. The rest of the extension builds on RFC 1869, the SMTP service extension mechanism, and RFC 1891 for the notifications it reports with.

sections.title: What Deliver By Is For
sections.content:
Throughout the RFC, the term deliver means the act of transmitting a message to its final destination by a message transport agent. Usually, but not always, that means storing or handing off the message to the recipient's mailbox. So an MTA that accepts a message to be delivered within a specified period is agreeing to store or hand off the message within that period. User-specified actions that might take place after the MTA hands the message over, such as a user-programmed filter that resends it somewhere else, are outside the scope of the term.

The extension lets an SMTP client ask the server to deliver the message within a prescribed period of time. The client also states what should happen if the message cannot be delivered in time: either the message is returned as undeliverable with no further processing, or a delayed delivery status notification is issued.

The RFC is careful that this is not a vehicle for requesting priority processing. A receiving server may assign whatever processing priority it wishes to a message sent with a Deliver By request. What the request does is express the message's urgency and add a degree of determinacy: an indication of the message's status within the given period may be requested and will be honoured, and the message may be withdrawn if it is not delivered within that period.

A typical use is to prevent delivery beyond a time that matters to the sender or recipient but is not known to the MTAs handling the message. The sender may know the message will be delivered as a page but not consider it important enough to page the recipient after business hours, so it can be marked so that delivery attempts are not made beyond 17:00. Another common use is to be told about delivery delays: the sender marks the message so that if it is not delivered within, say, 30 minutes, a delayed notification is generated while delivery attempts continue.
sections.plainLanguage: Deliver By says two things: a deadline in seconds, and what to do when the deadline passes. The server does not have to hurry the message, but it does have to report what happened, and it can withdraw the message if the time runs out.

sections.title: The Extension and How Support Is Checked
sections.content:
The extension uses the SMTP service extension mechanism. The name of the service extension is Deliver By, and the EHLO keyword value associated with it is DELIVERBY.

One optional parameter is allowed with that EHLO keyword, a comma separated list of options. Only one option is specified here, a min-by-time, which is a fixed integer giving the smallest by-time the server will accept when a by-mode of R is used. The syntax, in the augmented BNF notation of RFC 2234, is:

deliverby-param = min-by-time *( ',' extension-token )
min-by-time     = [1*9DIGIT]
extension-token = 1*<any CHAR excluding SP, COMMA and all control characters (US ASCII 0-31 inclusive)>

If the parameter is omitted, the server conveys no information about its fixed minimum by-time. One optional parameter using the keyword BY is added to the MAIL FROM command, and the maximum length of a MAIL FROM command line is increased by 17 characters to allow for the keyword and value. No additional SMTP verbs are defined by the extension.

A client that wants to use the extension issues the EHLO command to start an SMTP session and find out whether the server supports it. If the server replies with code 250 and the reply includes the EHLO keyword DELIVERBY, the extension is supported. If a numeric parameter follows the keyword, that number is the minimum by-time the server will accept for a by-mode of R, and any attempt to specify a by-mode of R with a by-time strictly below that limit is rejected with a permanent failure, a 55z reply code.

A server that supports the extension accepts the extended MAIL FROM command, and may return an error code if it determines that the request cannot be honoured. That may not become apparent to the server until the recipient addresses are presented with RCPT TO commands, or until the transfer of the message data is completed with the dot command. The server may therefore send a success response to MAIL FROM and only later return an error to RCPT TO, DATA or the dot command.
sections.plainLanguage: The extension is built into the standard way SMTP servers advertise what they can do. A server lists DELIVERBY in its greeting, optionally followed by the smallest deadline it will accept, and the client adds a BY parameter to the MAIL FROM line. A deadline below the server's minimum is refused straight away; otherwise the refusal can come later, after the recipients or the message body have been sent.

sections.title: The Extended MAIL FROM Command
sections.content:
The extended MAIL FROM command is identical to the MAIL FROM command of RFC 821 except that a BY parameter appears after the address. Its syntax is:

by-parameter = "BY="by-value
by-value     = by-time";"by-mode[by-trace]
by-time      = ["-" / "+"]1*9digit
by-mode      = "N" / "R"
by-trace     = "T"

The BY keyword must have an associated value. The by-time is a decimal number of seconds within which the message should be delivered, and it ranges from -999,999,999 to +999,999,999 seconds, which is enough to represent a time anywhere from about 31.6 years in the past to 31.6 years in the future. The by-mode says what the server must do if it cannot transmit the message within that many seconds, and the optional by-trace asks for a trace of the message's path.

The by-time is a delta time, the number of seconds within which to deliver the message. It does not extend an MTA's normal retention period for undeliverable messages, and it is not a deliver-after time. A delta time is used so that differences in system clocks between clients and servers cannot cause problems: a server converts the by-time into an absolute time, the deliver-by-time, by adding the by-time to its own current time. The transmission time of the MAIL FROM command is assumed to be instantaneous, so network latency introduces an error that slightly extends the effective by-time, and the more hops the message takes the more pronounced that effect becomes.

With a by-mode of N, the by-time may be zero or negative. That is not an error and should not be rejected; it says the deliver-by-time has already passed. Zero and negative values are allowed so that the requested delivery time is preserved, information the delivering MTA may want to include with the delivered message or show in a delivery or non-delivery notification. With a by-mode of R, a zero or negative by-time is a syntax error, and the server should answer with a 501 reply code, and with an enhanced error code of 5.5.4 if it supports those.

If the by-time is valid but the server cannot honour it for a server-specific reason, it should answer with 455 if the condition is transient, or 555 if it is permanent, along with a suitable enhanced error code.
sections.plainLanguage: The BY parameter has three parts: a number of seconds, a mode saying what to do if the time runs out, and an optional request for a trace. The number is a duration, not a clock time, so the client and server do not have to agree on what time it is.

sections.title: Server Behaviour and Relaying
sections.content:
When a valid BY parameter arrives, the server and its MTA follow a set of rules. Any delivery status notification generated for such a message should include the optional Arrival-Date field and the new Deliver-By-Date field.

If the message is delivered before the deliver-by-time, no special action is needed, except that a server which also supports the delivery status notification extension and was told to notify success must return a delivered notification. If the deliver-by-time has not yet passed and the message has proved undeliverable for temporary reasons, the server continues delivery or relay attempts according to the site's message handling policy, and it may return the message as undeliverable before the deadline if its own retention period is shorter than the by-time. If the message cannot be delivered for permanent reasons, the server must return a failed notification with an appropriate status for each recipient that asked for failure notifications.

When the deliver-by-time has been reached or passed, the two modes differ. With a by-mode of R, no further delivery attempts may be made and the server must issue a failed notification with status 5.4.7, delivery time expired. With a by-mode of N, the server continues delivery or relay attempts and must issue a delayed notification with status 4.4.7, delivery time expired.

Relaying has its own rules. If a message is relayed to a server that supports the extension, a new BY parameter must be relayed, giving the number of seconds remaining until the deliver-by-time, computed as close as reasonably possible to the time the MAIL FROM command is transmitted. If the deliver-by-time has already passed, the relayed by-time is negative, and that can only happen for a message with a by-mode of N. When a message carrying the by-trace value T is relayed, the relaying client should generate a relayed notification for each recipient that did not ask for no notifications; these relayed notifications are not terminal, and downstream servers may still send more.

A message with a by-mode of R must not be relayed to a server that does not support the extension, and the server it is relayed to must not have a fixed minimum by-time greater than the time remaining. If the message needs relaying to be delivered but cannot be relayed, it is deemed undeliverable for permanent reasons. A message with a by-mode of N may be relayed to any server, but when it is relayed to a server that does not support the extension, the relaying client must issue a relayed notification and should ask the next server for failure and delay notifications. For a foreign mail system, the request is conveyed if that system supports similar semantics, and otherwise the message is relayed as if to a server without the extension.
sections.plainLanguage: While there is time left, a temporary failure means keep trying, and a permanent failure means report failure. When the time runs out, return mode stops the attempts and reports a failure with status 5.4.7, while notify mode keeps trying and reports a delay with status 4.4.7. When the message is relayed, the deadline is passed on as the remaining number of seconds.

sections.title: The Deliver-By-Date Notification Field
sections.content:
The format of delivery status notifications is specified in RFC 1894, and notifications generated in response to a Deliver By request should include an Arrival-Date field. This memo extends the per-message fields of that format with a new field, Deliver-By-Date, giving the deliver-by-time as computed by the MTA or server generating the notification. In the augmented BNF of RFC 822, the per-message fields become:

per-message-fields =
    [ original-envelope-id-field CRLF ]
    reporting-mta-field CRLF
    [ dsn-gateway-field CRLF ]
    [ received-from-mta-field CRLF ]
    [ arrival-date-field CRLF ]
    [ deliver-by-date-field CRLF ]
    *( extension-field CRLF )
deliver-by-date-field = "Deliver-by-date" ":" date-time

The date-time value is an RFC 822 date-time field as amended by RFC 1123.
sections.plainLanguage: A delivery notification now has one more field, Deliver-By-Date, which records the deadline the server calculated. It sits next to the arrival date in the notification header.

sections.title: Example SMTP Dialogues
sections.content:
In the first example the client asks for the message to be delivered within 2 minutes, 120 seconds, and to be returned otherwise. The request takes the form of a BY parameter on the MAIL FROM line:

S: 220 acme.net SMTP server here
C: EHLO bigbiz.com
S: 250-acme.net
S: 250 DELIVERBY
C: MAIL FROM:<eljefe@bigbiz.com> BY=120;R
S: 250 <eljefe@bigbiz.com> sender ok
C: RCPT TO:<topbanana@other.com>
S: 250 <topbanana@wherever.com> recipient ok

In the second example the receiving server has to relay the message to mail.other.com. Because the by-mode is R, the message may only be relayed to a server that supports the extension, and the request must be relayed with it. When the relaying server connects, it learns the minimum by-time the next server will accept:

S: 220 mail.other.com ESMTP server at your service
C: EHLO acme.net
S: 250-mail.other.com
S: 250 DELIVERBY 240

That minimum is 4 minutes, 240 seconds, which exceeds the message's original by-time and therefore exceeds the remaining by-time. The relaying server therefore ends the SMTP session, after which it must either follow any other MX records or, if there are none left, return the message as undeliverable. The same outcome follows if the EHLO command met an error or did not include the DELIVERBY keyword.

In the third example the next server states a minimum of 30 seconds, which the remaining time can meet:

S: 220 mail.other.com ESMTP server at your service
C: EHLO acme.net
S: 250-mail.other.com
S: 250 DELIVERBY 30
C: MAIL FROM:<eljefe@bigbiz.com> BY=98;R
S: 250 <eljefe@bigbiz.com> Sender okay
C: RCPT TO:<topbanana@other.com>
S: 250 <topbanana@wherever.com> Recipient okay

Here the by-mode is preserved and the by-time is recomputed as the number of seconds remaining at the moment the MAIL FROM command went out. In this example 22 seconds have elapsed since the relaying server received the MAIL FROM line from the original client.
sections.plainLanguage: The examples show a client asking for delivery within two minutes, a relay that discovers the next server will not accept that deadline and has to give up, and a relay that recomputes the remaining time and passes it on.

sections.title: MX Records and Relaying
sections.content:
Sites that use the extension and direct their mail through MX records need to ensure that all of the MX hosts they direct mail to support the extension. A client that supports Deliver By should not go round trying several MX hosts looking for one that supports it.

MX hosts should pay careful attention to the min-by-time value they present in response to EHLO commands. It is not practical for an MX host to present a value that is substantially different from the one the destination host can handle, or that does not recognise the normal delivery latencies introduced when the MX host relays mail onwards.
sections.plainLanguage: Every mail server named in a domain's MX records has to support the extension, or a message with a deadline will be stuck. A server should also state a minimum that matches what it can really manage.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Implementing Deliver By allows a mail transport system to be traced. The by-trace field with value T explicitly requests a trace. Even when the by-trace field is not used, a crude trace can be produced by sending a series of messages with successively increasing by-time values, for example BY=0;R, BY=1;R and BY=2;R. Probing, and in some cases tracing, can also be done by querying the visible SMTP servers, by investigating Received header lines in bounced messages, and by using utilities such as traceroute.

On the other side, the RFC notes that servers supporting the extension are not required to give messages with a Deliver By request any special processing priority, and that the notifications generated for them are not required to be expedited either. A user should therefore not expect a message sent with a BY parameter to be handled faster, and sending BY=60;R does not guarantee that the sender will hear about a delivery failure within any particular time, because the notification itself is not necessarily expedited.
sections.plainLanguage: Deadlines leave a side channel: an observer can learn how long a message takes by trying a series of slightly different deadlines. The extension also does not make mail faster, and a failure report is not promised to come back quickly either.

items.label: Syntax error
items.desc: A by-time of zero or less was sent with a by-mode of R.

items.label: Transient failure
items.desc: The by-time is valid but the server cannot honour it for a transient reason.

items.label: Permanent failure
items.desc: The by-time is valid but the server cannot honour it for a permanent reason.

items.label: Permanent failure
items.desc: The by-time is below the minimum the server stated for a by-mode of R.

items.label: Delayed notification status
items.desc: Delivery time expired, sent when a by-mode of N reaches the deadline.

items.label: Failed notification status
items.desc: Delivery time expired, sent when a by-mode of R reaches the deadline.
